summary: The note is a Wikipedia-style article on pearls. It covers the history of pearl diving, from prehistoric origins and extensive Han Dynasty hunting in the South China Sea to Ibn Battuta's 14th-century description in the Arabian Sea. It then explains what a pearl is, its calcium carbonate composition and shape variations, and its value as a gem and metaphor for rarity.
one_line: Overview of pearls: their formation in mollusks, composition, shapes, and the history of pearl diving in the Indian Ocean and China.
key_facts: For thousands of years, seawater pearls were retrieved by divers in the Indian Ocean in areas such as the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Mannar.
Evidence suggests a prehistoric origin to pearl diving in the Indian Ocean regions.
Starting in the Han Dynasty (206 BC -- 220 AD), the Chinese hunted extensively for seawater pearls in the South China Sea.
The traveller Ibn Battuta provided the earliest known description of pearl diving in the 14th-century Arabian Sea, in which a cord was attached to the diver's waist.
A pearl is a hard glistening object produced within the soft tissue (specifically the mantle) of a living shelled mollusk or another animal, such as a conulariid.
A pearl is composed of calcium carbonate, mainly aragonite or a mixture of aragonite and calcite, in minute crystalline form.
The calcium carbonate of a pearl is deposited in concentric layers, as in the shell of a mollusk.
The ideal pearl is perfectly round and smooth, but many other shapes, known as baroque pearls, can occur.
The finest quality natural pearls have been highly valued as gemstones and objects of beauty for many centuries.
Because of its value, pearl has become a metaphor for something rare, fine, admirable and valuable.
